strengths: Identifies and rigorously documents a novel and consistent phenomenon ('Imitation Shock') across a wide array of settings (different teachers, datasets, dataset scales, student backbones, and domains in Figure 2/Appendix B), lending credibility that this is a real, reproducible training-dynamics artifact rather than a one-off anomaly.

Provides a fairly thorough causal/mechanistic investigation rather than just a correlational observation: checkpoint-wise one-step interventions (Figure 5), 'train-other-tokens-only' ablation (Figure 4b), and the 4x4 loss-transfer matrix (Table 8) collectively build a coherent story for why anchor tokens suppress yet-to-learn tokens.

Directly tests and rules out simpler static alternatives (initial confidence, gradient-sketch similarity) as explanations for the anchor/non-anchor split (Section 4.5, Appendices F-G), strengthening the claim that trajectory information is genuinely necessary.

The proposed method (T3S) is simple, is extended to both AR and diffusion LLM training regimes with sensible task-specific instantiations (masking vs. union-masking), and shows large, consistent improvements over SFT and the RRT baseline across two datasets and two teachers.

Practical/impressive headline results (small student models approaching or exceeding much larger/frontier teacher performance with only hundreds of examples) and additional supporting analyses (cross-model transfer of token masks, inference-efficiency gains in the dLLM setting) add practical significance.
weaknesses: The core evaluation relies almost entirely on AIME24/AIME25 (two small, high-variance competition math benchmarks) with only 200-training-example, 50-step regimes; while some OOD/forgetting benchmarks are reported in the appendix, the paper's headline claims (e.g., 'surpasses DeepSeek-R1', 'approaches Qwen3-235B') are drawn from this narrow evaluation, which limits confidence that the gains generalize broadly.

There is a practical circularity/leakage concern: the Imitation Bottleneck used to define the anchor/yet-to-learn token partition is identified using training-accuracy trajectories that themselves come from a completed full training run (or require gold-answer/verifier access), so the method as validated is not obviously separable from hindsight information; Section 3.6 asserts an online variant is feasible but this is not empirically demonstrated.

No variance/error bars or statistical significance are reported for the main results tables (Table 3, 4, 5) despite AIME scores being averaged over only 16 rollouts on 200-prompt subsets, which are known to be noisy; this makes it hard to assess how robust the reported gains (often only a few points) truly are.

Baseline comparisons are limited to standard SFT and the authors' own RRT method; no comparison to other established token-selection/data-efficiency baselines (e.g., RHO-1-style selective LM, entropy/forking-token RL selection methods cited in Related Work) is included in the main quantitative results, only briefly discussed qualitatively.

The dLLM experiments use only a single base model (LLaDA-2.0-Mini), a single teacher, and three evaluation benchmarks, which is a fairly thin evidence base for the strong claim of 'state-of-the-art performance among all 16B-scale no-think models.'

The threshold τ for dLLM token selection appears to be tuned post hoc on the same evaluation set used for reporting results (Table 7), raising a mild concern about selection bias in hyperparameter choice without a held-out validation protocol.

strengths: Identifies and characterizes an interesting empirical phenomenon ('Imitation Shock') across a reasonably broad set of settings (different teachers, datasets, dataset scales, student models, and domains in Figure 2/Appendix B), lending some credibility that the crash-then-recover pattern is not a one-off artifact.

The causal/interventional evidence for anchor-induced suppression (checkpoint-wise one-step intervention in Figure 5, and the loss-transfer asymmetry matrix in Table 8) goes beyond pure correlation and provides a plausible mechanistic account for why anchor and non-anchor tokens interfere.

Reasonably thorough set of control experiments in the appendix (static-confidence masking baselines, gradient-sketch visualization, base-confidence scatter) that attempt to rule out simpler alternative explanations (e.g., that anchors are just low/high initial-confidence tokens).
The method is extended beyond AR models to diffusion LLMs with a sensible adaptation (union masking of bottleneck-candidate tokens), showing some generality of the underlying idea.
Practical overhead is modest and the method could plausibly be integrated into existing pipelines that already track training-set accuracy or verifier signals.
weaknesses: Evaluation is very narrow: almost all headline claims (Qwen3-8B 'surpassing' DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-32B 'approaching' Qwen3-235B) rest on just two competition-math benchmarks (AIME24/25) with only 200 training prompts and 50 optimization steps, raising strong concerns about overfitting to a narrow test distribution rather than genuine reasoning improvement.

No training-seed variance is reported for the central comparisons (Table 3, Table 4): AIME scores are averaged over 16 inference rollouts, but it is unclear whether the distillation runs themselves (data order, single seed) were repeated, which is critical given the paper's own finding that these small-scale training trajectories are highly non-monotonic and sensitive (Imitation Shock itself demonstrates high checkpoint-to-checkpoint volatility).

The dLLM threshold τ appears to be selected by directly optimizing AIME25 score (Table 7), i.e., a hyperparameter tuned on the same benchmark used to report final performance, which is a methodologically questionable form of test-set tuning that undermines the reliability of the 'state-of-the-art among 16B no-think models' claim.

Comparisons across model families with very different architectures, sizes, and training recipes (e.g., LLaDA-2.0-Mini vs. Qwen3-14B, Ministral-14B, Ling-Mini, Qwen3-30B-A3B) are used to support strong claims of state-of-the-art status, but these are not controlled comparisons and conflate many confounding factors beyond the proposed method.

The qualitative word-cloud evidence for anchor vs. non-anchor tokens (Figure 3) is unconvincing: the displayed tokens (e.g., 'Rotation', 'Directed', 'Conflict' vs. 'probably', 'Minus') do not obviously correspond to any intuitive notion of 'imitation surface pattern' vs. 'reasoning-relevant' tokens, weakening the qualitative narrative.

The extreme collapse of the -T3S ablation (e.g., from ~71 to ~28 average score) is surprisingly severe and is not fully explained; it is unclear whether this reflects a genuine antagonistic partition or an artifact of extreme training instability at only 50 steps with masked majority tokens.

The method's core selection signal (training accuracy to locate the Imitation Bottleneck) requires gold answers/verifiers, restricting applicability to verifiable domains, and the paper's dismissal of this limitation is somewhat superficial given that many valuable distillation targets (open-ended reasoning, dialogue, non-verifiable domains) would not support this mechanism.

Related work on token-level selection (Rho-1, entropy-based RLVR token selection, critical-token DPO methods) is discussed but never directly compared as a baseline beyond simple top-p confidence masking, leaving open whether T3S actually outperforms more sophisticated existing token-selection alternatives.

The paper makes very strong claims ('surpasses DeepSeek-R1', 'approaches Qwen3-235B', 'achieves SOTA among 16B-scale no-think models') that are disproportionate to the narrow experimental scope (few hundred examples, 1-2 benchmarks, apparently single-seed training runs), which raises concerns about the robustness and reproducibility of the central empirical claims.

strengths: Identifies and thoroughly characterizes a novel and reproducible phenomenon ('Imitation Shock'/'Imitation Bottleneck') across a genuinely broad sweep of settings (different teachers, datasets, dataset scales, student backbones, and domains, Figure 2), which strengthens the claim that the effect is not an artifact of one configuration.

Provides multiple complementary lines of evidence for the causal mechanism rather than relying on correlation alone: the Recovering-Residual-Transfer experiment (Table 1), the checkpoint-wise one-step anchor-only gradient intervention (Figure 5), and the controlled loss-transfer matrix (Table 8) together build a reasonably convincing mechanistic story of anchor-induced suppression.

Careful ablations distinguish trajectory-based targeting from simpler static heuristics: masking by base-model confidence (highest/lowest) and gradient-sketch/t-SNE visualizations both fail to separate anchors from yet-to-learn tokens or to remove Imitation Shock (Appendix F, G), supporting the necessity of the trajectory signal specifically.

The method generalizes across two quite different paradigms (AR masking vs. union masking for dLLMs), and the empirical payoff is substantial: Qwen3-8B surpassing its DeepSeek-R1 teacher, Qwen3-32B approaching Qwen3-235B, and a T3S-trained LLaDA-2.0-Mini reported as SOTA among 16B-scale no-think models, all using only hundreds of examples.
Diagnostic -T3S ablation (inverting the mask) causes severe collapse, which is a strong sanity check that the selected token partition is functionally meaningful rather than an arbitrary subset.

Reasonable breadth of secondary analyses (OOD reasoning/forgetting mitigation, cross-model transferability of yet-to-learn tokens, inference-efficiency gains for dLLMs, sensitivity to τ) that round out the picture and pre-empt several natural follow-up questions.
weaknesses: All core experiments use extremely small data regimes (200 examples, 50 optimization steps, essentially near-full-batch training with batch size 64), and it is unclear whether the 'Imitation Bottleneck' concept and its detection via training accuracy remain well-defined or practically computable in standard large-scale continual pretraining/distillation with far larger corpora and much noisier per-checkpoint accuracy; the one larger-scale example (65K samples) is shown only qualitatively (Figure 2c) without a corresponding quantitative T3S result at that scale.

The method's core dependency on per-checkpoint training accuracy to locate the bottleneck requires dense checkpointing and reliable gold-answer/verifier signals; while the authors argue this matches RL/verifier pipelines, no wall-clock or compute-overhead numbers are given for realistic large-model settings, leaving practical scalability of the online-monitoring proposal (Section 3.6) largely unverified.

Statistical rigor is limited: scores are averages over 16 sampling runs but no variance/confidence intervals are reported for the main tables, making it hard to judge whether some of the smaller gains (e.g., some OOD/forgetting deltas in Appendix D, which are often <1 point) are meaningful.

No direct empirical comparison to existing token-priority baselines discussed in Related Work (e.g., RHO-1 selective language modeling, critical/forking-token RLVR methods) beyond the two static-confidence masking ablations constructed by the authors themselves; a head-to-head comparison against a published token-selection baseline would better substantiate the originality/significance claims.

The impressive teacher-mixing results (Table 4, Qwen3-8B > DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-32B ≈ Qwen3-235B) are obtained and evaluated almost entirely on the same AIME24/25 benchmarks used to tune/validate the method, raising some risk that gains are partly benchmark-specific; the OOD evaluation in Appendix D is somewhat reassuring but shows more modest, occasionally negligible improvements.

The 'anchor tokens cannot coexist with yet-to-learn tokens' claim, while supported by the loss-transfer matrix, is drawn from a single dataset/model configuration (BOBA-200, Qwen3-8B/R1); it would strengthen the causal claim to replicate this specific asymmetry experiment across at least one more teacher-student-dataset combination.

The dLLM extension introduces an additional sensitive hyperparameter τ that must be tuned (Table 7 shows a fairly narrow effective range), adding practical complexity that is not deeply analyzed beyond one sensitivity sweep on one benchmark.

strengths: Identifies and thoroughly documents a novel, reproducible phenomenon ('Imitation Shock') across a wide range of settings: different teachers, datasets, dataset scales, student architectures, and training domains (Figure 2, Appendix E), lending credibility that this is a real and general training dynamic rather than an artifact of one setup.

Provides multiple complementary and largely causal lines of evidence for the proposed mechanism: recovering-residual transfer (Table 1), token-level confidence bifurcation (Figure 4), one-step anchor-only gradient intervention (Figure 5), gradient norm/cosine-similarity analysis (Figure 6), and a controlled loss-transfer matrix (Table 6) — together these build a coherent and reasonably rigorous causal story rather than a purely correlational one.

The proposed method (T3S) is simple to implement, cheap (uses existing checkpoints, no extra models needed beyond a token selector), and is validated with strong ablations: comparisons against RRT, an inverted-mask diagnostic (-T3S), static-confidence-based masking baselines (Appendix K), robustness to imperfect bottleneck selection (Table 8), and cross-model transferability of token targets (Appendix C).

Demonstrates generality beyond the primary AR setting by extending the method to diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) with a principled adaptation (union masking), yielding a strong, competitive standalone dLLM and improved inference efficiency.

Empirical gains are large and consistently reported across many axes (different teachers, larger-scale data, cross-family students, code domain, OOD reasoning and forgetting benchmarks), suggesting the effect is not narrowly tuned to a single benchmark.
weaknesses: The headline claims (e.g., Qwen3-8B 'surpassing' DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-32B 'approaching' Qwen3-235B using only ~200-600 examples and 50 optimization steps) are extraordinary and evaluated almost exclusively on AIME24/25, a small, heavily-used, and contamination-prone benchmark; broader, more diverse and larger held-out evaluation would strengthen confidence that this reflects genuine reasoning improvement rather than benchmark-specific overfitting.

The bottleneck/anchor identification procedure requires gold-standard training accuracy (a verifier), which the paper acknowledges but does not fully explore how performance degrades when only noisy or partial verification signals are available, limiting applicability to non-verifiable domains.

Reported results are point estimates (averaged over 16 generation runs) without variance across independent training/distillation runs, making it hard to assess how sensitive the large reported gains are to training-run stochasticity, especially given very small training sets and few optimization steps.

The definition and role of the 'AR token selector model M0' used for confidence profiling (particularly for dLLMs) is not fully specified in the main text, and details about whether/how it differs from the model being trained are only partially clarified in the appendix.

The paper's presentation is dense, with many acronyms, takeaways, and appendices; core experimental protocol details (dataset construction, correctness criteria, hyperparameters for many ablations) are relegated to appendices, which can hinder a self-contained understanding of the main claims.

While the token partition is shown to be non-recoverable by static confidence or local gradient similarity, the explanation for *why* certain tokens become anchors (linguistic/semantic characteristics, e.g., the word clouds in Figure 3) is left largely descriptive rather than mechanistically or theoretically grounded.

strengths: The paper documents an interesting and seemingly reproducible empirical phenomenon ('Imitation Shock': loss falls monotonically while task accuracy crashes then recovers) across a reasonably diverse set of settings (different teachers, datasets, dataset scales, student backbones, and domains in Fig. 2), which is a novel observational contribution.

Extensive mechanistic probing is offered to support the token-level story: recovering-residual transfer (Table 1), token confidence bifurcation (Fig. 4), causal one-step intervention on anchor tokens (Fig. 5), gradient norm/cosine-similarity analysis (Fig. 6), and a controlled loss-transfer matrix (Table 6) all point in a consistent direction, which strengthens the internal narrative.

The proposed T3S method is simple to implement (masking tokens by trajectory-based confidence change) and is extended non-trivially to the diffusion-LLM setting via union masking, showing the idea is not limited to one architecture.

A large number of robustness/ablation studies are included (bottleneck-selector sensitivity in Table 8, fixed-heuristic selector T3S-simple in Table 7, static-confidence baselines in Table 19, cross-model transfer of anchor sets in Table 9, comparisons to GKD/SWITCH/Mix-Distillation), which is commendable diligence for an initial empirical study.
weaknesses: Core practicality/circularity problem: the Imitation Bottleneck θb is defined as the argmin of training accuracy over the *entire* observed trajectory (Eq. 1). Identifying this checkpoint therefore requires having already trained through and past the bottleneck to see the subsequent recovery, which conflicts with the paper's claim (Sec. 3.5) that this can be done 'online... mirroring early stopping.' Early stopping does not require knowledge of a future minimum; this method does. The T3S-simple heuristic (fixed step 10) partially sidesteps this, but the main method as formalized has an unresolved chicken-and-egg issue that is not adequately addressed.

All experiments are conducted in an extremely low-step/low-data regime (50 optimization steps, batch size 64, ~200–3200 examples, with one scale-up experiment at ~100K). It is unclear whether the crash-then-recover pattern and the anchor/non-anchor dichotomy are fundamental properties of continual distillation or largely an artifact of this specific tiny-step, high-effective-LR regime; no experiments test many-epoch/large-scale standard fine-tuning pipelines where per-step dynamics of this kind are typically smoothed out.

Headline claims ('Qwen3-8B surpasses DeepSeek-R1', 'Qwen3-32B approaches Qwen3-235B') rest almost entirely on AIME24/AIME25, which contain only ~30 problems each; despite 16-run averaging, these are narrow, high-variance, competition-math-specific benchmarks. The more broadly scoped OOD evaluation (Table 12) shows much more modest average gains (~2–3 points), suggesting the 'surpasses the teacher' narrative is benchmark-specific and somewhat overstated relative to the paper's framing.

The dLLM 'state-of-the-art among 16B-scale no-think models' claim (Table 5) compares against a heterogeneous set of models with different pretraining data, architectures, and training recipes (Ministral, Ling-Mini, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-30B-A3B), which is not a controlled comparison and undermines the strength of the SOTA claim.

No variance/error bars are reported for the checkpoint-level trajectory plots (Figs. 1–6) or for most ablation tables; the central phenomenon is illustrated largely via single training runs per setting, so it is unclear how robust the precise bifurcation/bottleneck location is to random seed.

The paper is dense with many 'Takeaways' and appendix analyses (12 appendix sections) that dilute focus; some analyses (e.g., Section 2.3's 'train other tokens only' intervention) are close to re-deriving the proposed method itself, making the causal narrative feel partly self-confirming rather than independently validating the mechanism.

Baseline comparisons against established token-priority/distillation methods (GKD, SWITCH, Mix Distillation) are restricted to tokenizer-sharing settings, limiting the generality of claims that T3S outperforms prior token-selection approaches in the OOD-teacher regime that is central to the paper's motivation.

Key hyperparameters (mask fraction ~20% for AR, τ=0.2 for dLLM) appear tuned post-hoc via sensitivity sweeps on the same evaluation benchmarks used for reporting final results, raising concerns about selection bias in the reported numbers.

strengths: Identifies and rigorously characterizes a novel and practically important phenomenon ("Imitation Shock") in continual reasoning distillation, showing that training loss can decrease monotonically while all performance metrics crash and recover at a shared 'Imitation Bottleneck.'

Provides a compelling multi-pronged mechanistic account: token confidence bifurcation (Fig. 4), causal one-step intervention showing anchor-induced suppression (Fig. 5), gradient-norm/cosine-similarity analysis (Fig. 6), and a controlled loss-transfer matrix (Table 6) all converge on the same anchor-vs-yet-to-learn-token story, giving strong triangulated evidence rather than a single correlational observation.

The proposed method (T3S) is simple, cheap to implement (a masking scheme derived from bottleneck-referenced token confidence), and is evaluated across a wide range of settings: different teachers (DeepSeek-R1, QWQ), datasets (BOBA-200, S1K-200), dataset scales (200 to ~100K), student model families (Qwen3, Llama3-derived), and domains (math, code).

Strong empirical results with only hundreds of training examples: Qwen3-8B surpasses its teacher DeepSeek-R1 on AIME, Qwen3-32B approaches Qwen3-235B, and extension to diffusion LLMs (LLaDA-2.0-Mini) yields state-of-the-art results among 16B-scale no-think models, along with inference efficiency gains.

Careful ablations addressing alternative explanations: static confidence/entropy-based masking baselines are shown to fail and still exhibit Imitation Shock (Appendix K), and gradient-sketch/initial-confidence overlap analyses (Appendix J) show the anchor/non-anchor split is not recoverable from single-checkpoint signals, strengthening the claim that trajectory-awareness is essential.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility details (hyperparameters, dataset construction, teacher sampling protocol) are provided in the appendix, and sensitivity analyses (bottleneck selector robustness, τ threshold for dLLM) support practical robustness of the method.
weaknesses: Primary evaluation relies heavily on AIME24/25, which are small benchmarks (30 problems each); although scores are averaged over 16 runs, variance/confidence intervals are not reported, making it hard to assess statistical significance of relatively small differences (e.g., T3S vs. RRT gaps of 1-3 points).

The claim that Qwen3-8B "surpasses DeepSeek-R1" and Qwen3-32B "approaches Qwen3-235B" is based on a narrow set of competition-math benchmarks; broader capability comparisons (e.g., general reasoning, coding, knowledge) are comparatively less extensively validated, so the headline claims may overstate generality.

Training data scale (mostly 200 examples, 50 steps) is very small, and while some scale-up experiments exist in the appendix (3K, ~100K), the core mechanistic analyses (Imitation Shock characterization, token dynamics) are conducted almost exclusively in this very low-data regime, leaving open how the phenomenon and method behave in more standard large-scale distillation/post-training pipelines.

The bottleneck-identification procedure requires training-set accuracy (i.e., gold answers or a verifier) at every checkpoint, which the paper concedes is a practical requirement; though framed as similar to early stopping, this still adds nontrivial overhead and dependency on a reliable correctness signal that may not always be available or cheap.

The τ threshold for dLLM masking and other hyperparameters appear to be tuned directly on evaluation benchmarks (e.g., AIME25 in Table 11), raising a risk of overfitting to the test set rather than validating on a held-out split.

Some strong causal/mechanistic language (e.g., "gradients... cannot coexist," "root cause") is used somewhat loosely; while the interventions are suggestive and informative, they do not fully rule out confounds (e.g., masking-induced changes in effective batch composition or learning-rate dynamics per token could partly explain observed effects).

The paper is very dense with many claims and figures compressed into a short main text, with most quantitative rigor (e.g., loss-transfer matrix, cross-model transfer) relegated to the appendix; a clearer articulation of the core method (Section 3) relative to the extensive motivating analysis (Section 2) would improve readability.
